speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Ms Grace Fu, Minister for National Development Mr Desmond Lee and I will be making Ministerial Statements to address the issues raised.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our Statements will address Question Nos 1 to 27 for oral answer and Question Nos 65 to 67 for written answer, in today’s Order Paper, as well as related questions that have been filed for subsequent Sittings.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They worked well together and responded effectively to mitigate the impact of the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have completed the first phase of the clean-up operations, including the operations at sea.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have now moved to the next phase, which involves more focused cleaning of difficult-to-reach areas.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The removal of the remaining fuel oil from the damaged vessel is ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) was notified at 2.22 pm and its first patrol craft arrived at the incident site 11 minutes later at 2.33 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Upon confirming that a significant amount of oil had spilled into the water, the patrol craft sprayed dispersantd in the surrounding areas.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This needs to be done quickly, so that the dispersantd can start to break down the oil, which will facilitate subsequent cleaning operations at sea and on land.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Otherwise, the oil will harden over time and become more difficult to remove.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides the initial patrol vessel, 11 more vessels from MPA and their contractors were deployed to perform different roles during the initial phase of the response on 14 June.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA also checked the damaged vessel to ensure that it would not sink, the crew were safe and there was no further spillage of oil.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA then activated T&T Salvage Asia to lay heavy-duty containment booms around the damaged vessel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: T&T’s vessel arrived at the incident location at 9.41 pm on 14 June, as it took a few hours to load the vessel with the heavy equipment and another few hours to sail to the incident site.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Despite the challenges of working at night and under bad weather conditions, T&T did well to deploy 200 metres of oil booms around the damaged vessel by working through the night.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The deployment of the oil booms was completed at 5.15 am on 15 June.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For such spills, the patrol vessel will focus on spraying dispersants and deploy contractors to lay heavy-duty oil containment booms around the damaged vessel as a preventive measure in case there is further spillage of oil from the vessel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I had explained during last week’s joint press conference that the main purpose of the containment booms around the damaged vessel was not to “fence in” all the spilled oil.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When there is a sudden discharge of a large amount of oil, like what happened on 14 June, the spilled oil will not remain stationary at the incident site.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will be carried by tidal currents and waves to other locations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The containment booms were therefore intended as a preventive measure in case there was further oil spillage from the damaged vessel.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The containment boomd can also help to catch some of the oil spill which remained in the vicinity of the incident location and did not float elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But this is not 100% foolproof, because the tidal currents and waves can carry the oil to go below or above the booms.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition to laying containment booms around the damaged vessel, we also deployed oil skimmers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Based on guidance from industry experts such as the ITOPF, oil skimmers are most effective against large and thick patches of oil.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence, before deploying the skimmers, MPA and its contractors had to first confirm the location of the large oil patches.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This task was challenging for a number of reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, due to thundery showers on 14 June afternoon, visibility was poor and the vessels from MPA and their contractors were not able to spot large patches of oil in the sea in the first few hours after the incident.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, as the density of the spilled oil in this case is very close to that of seawater, the oil slicks might have gone below the water surface, making detection harder.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When night fell, the reduced visibility made it even more difficult for MPA and its contractors to locate the spilled oil.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Throughout its response, MPA used a multi-pronged approach involving drones, satellite imagery and sightings from ships at sea and personnel on the ground to confirm the location of large oil patches.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the morning of 15 June, when large oil patches were located, MPA deployed oil skimmers to skim the oil from the sea.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPA and its contractors also carried out the targeted deployment of booms along our coastlines and waterfronts to facilitate clean-up operations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This approach ensures the booms are placed where they can be most effective.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In response to Mr Louis Chua’s question, MPA did not prioritise oil collection in certain areas before deploying booms to contain the spill.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To Mr Christopher de Souza’s question, our contractors also used absorbent booms with hydrophobic content.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our clean-up methods and operations are guided by international experts from ITOPF, and our agencies work closely with specialised companies and contractors who have strong track records in responding to oil spills.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We work with them on the deployment of assets to ensure optimal outcomes, taking into account factors such as the geography of the area, weather conditions, prevailing winds and tidal conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our agencies had provided regular updates from the day of the incident on 14 June.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our approach is to push out relevant information to the public as soon as possible, such as information on air and water quality, while we continue with the operations at sea and on land to deal with an evolving situation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Minister Grace Fu, Minister Desmond Lee and I also provided updates on the management and impact of the oil spill in the days following the incident.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Please allow me to elaborate on the communications timeline.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the afternoon of 14 June, MPA informed the other agencies of the oil spillage.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: After being alerted, the agencies mobilised their staff to actively monitor the situation and stood ready to respond.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At around 9.20 pm, the Sentosa Development Corporation (SDC) began to cordon off affected parts of Palawan beach, when they first sighted oil on the beach.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At 10.59 am, SDC published a post on their Facebook page and website to inform the public that the waters of Tanjong, Palawan and Siloso Beach on Sentosa were closed for clean-up operations, but the three beaches remained open.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At 1.44 pm, MPA notified the public via a media statement that patches of oil and light sheens were observed off Pasir Panjang terminal and along Sentosa beaches.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Later that day, at 7.33 pm, a joint media statement was issued by the agencies to inform the public that oil had also landed along shorelines in other areas and that affected beaches would be closed to facilitate clean-up operations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The statement highlighted that the agencies were taking action to mitigate the effects of the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These media statements and other updates were also posted on the social media platforms of the agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some Members have asked about possible measures to prevent oil spills in future.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, we have taken steps to enhance the safety of vessels and bunkering operations to minimise the risks of accidents and oil spills in our waters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have also put in place practices such as mandatory safety training and shipboard drills for vessel crew on incident response as well as inspections for vessels in our port to ensure compliance with international safety conventions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While we do our best to reduce the risks, oil spills may still happen in our waters or in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is not possible to completely eliminate this risk.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Therefore, we have prepared for and maintained our readiness to respond in a prompt, coordinated and effective manner when such incidents occur.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have worked with industry partners to develop a contingency plan, which we rehearse and refine every two years during our inter-agency exercises for oil spills.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our standard operating procedures (SOPs) were enhanced along the way and they helped us to respond to this incident effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to update and improve our SOPs and contingency plans with learning points from this incident and prepare our teams to deal with oil spills effectively through training and regular inter-agency exercises.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is more work ahead to complete the next phase of the clean-up operations and to mitigate the impact of the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Let us continue to work closely together, so that we can return to normalcy as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I call on the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, Ms Grace Fu.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I will address the progress of our land-based clean-ups, the challenges involved, our emphasis on protecting the health and well-being of our workers and the public, the impact to the businesses and our efforts in monitoring any impact on the safety of our food, air and water quality.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have made good progress in cleaning up the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The bulk of oil-soaked sand has been removed and sent to toxic waste treatment facilities for safe treatment and disposal.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Booms have also been deployed to prevent oil from being washed ashore or into our inland canals.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This operation will not have been possible without the tireless and coordinated efforts from multiple agencies and many service providers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several Members have raised questions about the welfare and safety of our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have been taking many steps to ensure their safety and well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As part of its air quality monitoring regime, NEA monitors ambient levels of volatile organic compounds, or VOCs, through our network of 24/7 ambient air monitoring stations at various locations in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: One of the monitoring stations is located on Sentosa and there is also one at the eastern-end of East Coast Park.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The monitoring stations did not detect any anomalies over this period of time, including for benzene, toluene and xylene, or BTX, that are commonly associated with bunkering fuels and other petrochemicals.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When the oil slick reached stretches of our coastline on 15 June, NEA began conducting daily air quality tests using mobile detectors at affected areas of East Coast Park, Sentosa and Labrador Nature Reserve to ensure the safety of the public and clean-up personnel.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Miss Rachel Ong1 asked if there were health and safety concerns from breathing in the oil fumes.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I have explained that the air quality at affected areas is safe, based on both measurements from our 24/7 ambient air monitoring stations as well as localised daily testing using mobile detectors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While members of the public near the beachfront or shoreline may experience odour from time to time, especially in the early days of the oil spill, it is safe to be around these areas.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, as part of the SOP, service providers are involved in our oil spill response in many critical functions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many of them are specialised contractors involved in the laying of booms and in cleaning of difficult-to-clean areas, such as rock bunds.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Others are general cleaning contractors involved in clearing the beaches of oily sand and debris.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These service providers participate in our regular oil spill exercises and are familiar with their roles and processes.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Before deployment, personnel are briefed on their tasks and workplace safety.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Agencies and their contractors are regularly reminded to ensure that sufficient rest breaks and rehydration are provided.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also reminded cleaning contractors to ensure that workers receive rest days and consider rotating workers, where possible.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Workers who feel unwell should approach their employer for support and assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Louis Ng, Ms He Ting Ru, Mr Melvin Yong and Miss Rachel Ong2 asked about the provision of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As is the case for any work carried out in Singapore, employers, including the contractors, are responsible for assessing the site conditions, nature of tasks and risks when deploying and equipping their workers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the immediate few days after the oil spill, when a sizeable amount of oil was washed up on shore, NEA issued a general advisory for personnel involved in the clean-up effort to include masks, goggles, rubber gloves and high waterproof boots as part of their PPE.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This was done as an additional precaution even though the air quality was well within safe levels.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: After the bulk of the oil was removed, NEA updated the advisory to no longer require masks and goggles.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The first phase of the clean-up focused on removing the oil slicks and contaminated sand from the surface of affected beaches and deploying booms to avoid further contamination.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All the remaining affected areas have entered the second phase of the clean-up response, which focuses on difficult to clean areas like rock bunds, breakwaters and oil trapped deeper in the sand.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members of the public may notice a scaling down of general cleaning at the beaches, as more specialised teams are deployed to clean these difficult areas.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: General cleaning of the beaches may still be required, as oil remnants may continue to be washed ashore.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The cleaning methods for the second phase have been decided jointly between the oil spill consultants and the cleaning contractors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These methods may be refined along the way as the shoreline of each affected area may be different.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For ecologically-sensitive locations, the National Parks Board (NParks) is consulted on the methods to be deployed.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: ONE°15 Marina and the Marina at Keppel Bay have reopened as clean-up efforts continue to progress.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will test the water quality to ensure that it is back to normal and stable for at least a week before resuming swimming and other primary-contact sea activities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Agencies have been monitoring the situation carefully and closely.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We understand the frustration and inconvenience that businesses have experienced due to the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: That is why SDC, which manages Sentosa and businesses on the Southern Islands, and other agencies, such as NParks, that collectively manage the beachfront along East Coast Park, have been proactively reaching out to their tenants.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: SDC will also look to promote a return of footfall through marketing and social media support.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As mentioned by the Ministry of Transport (MOT) during last week's joint press conference, the economic losses resulting from the oil spill can be accessed for claims.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Contact details of the insurer have been made available to the public.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many volunteers have stepped forward to offer their assistance in the clean-up operations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Volunteers have not been directly involved in the beach clean-up actions, due to the complexity of the tasks and for their personal safety.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin asked how citizens can be involved in our clean-up efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are considering mobilising volunteers for the final phase of the clean-up, where remnant oil deposits hardened and mixed with sand in the form of tar balls will need to be sieved and separated for removal.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This process is labour-intensive and if we have more hands to help, we can relieve the cleaners and accelerate the reopening of the beaches.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If and when volunteers are mobilised, we will tap on those who have registered with NParks as well as many volunteer groups who have contacted me personally and the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) through social media and WhatsApp after assessing that it is safe to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Public Hygiene Council will help to train, equip and coordinate with volunteers for this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This would be a safe and meaningful way for Singaporeans to contribute to the reopening of our beaches.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I will now address questions on food safety and water quality, which Miss Cheryl Chan, Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Xie Yao Quan have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To date, our fish farms remain unaffected by the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Nonetheless, as a precautionary measure, the Singapore Food Agency has been taking seafood samples from coastal fish farms in the East Johor Strait for food safety tests.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are also monitoring the quality of imported fish and seafood.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Miss Rachel Ong3 asked if real-time data from the Marine Environment Sensing Network (MESN) buoys can be made available on an hourly basis to fish farms and relevant non-governmental organisations' communities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I understand that MESN currently deploys one buoy at St John's Island and real-time data that has been assessed to be of high confidence is publicly accessible on MESN's online data platform.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: There has been no impact to our water supply.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Sensors at our five desalination plants, including at the Jurong Island Desalination Plant closest to the oil spill location, continue to show no abnormalities in the quality of seawater.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the event that any plant in Singapore's water supply system is disrupted, the Public Utilities Board (PUB) will step up production capacity in our remaining plants.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also deployed booms to prevent oil leaks from reaching the shore or flowing inland.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Here, I would like to express sincere gratitude to various Government agencies and cleaning contractors.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Thanks to their close coordination and relentless efforts, the cleanup work has proceeded smoothly.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To ensure public safety and the safety of cleaning personnel, we have implemented a series of measures.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the areas affected by oil pollution, we have conducted air quality tests to ensure the personal safety of nearby residents, tourists and clean-up personnel.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The air quality has remained at safe levels.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Before commencing the clean-up work, we briefed the personnel on the work scope and safety measures, and provided them with appropriate personal protective equipment.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also ensured that the personnel have sufficient rest time and regularly replenish their fluids.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The beaches at Sentosa, East Coast Park and the Southern Islands will be gradually reopened to the public for land-based activities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will conduct water quality tests to ensure that water quality is restored to normal and remain stable for at least one week before allowing swimming and water activities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are also considering mobilising volunteers to participate in the final phase of the clean-up work, to lighten the burden on the cleaning personnel and expedite the reopening of beaches.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Relevant authorities have been closely monitoring the situation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We understand that the oil spill incident has caused inconvenience to some businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Affected businesses and relevant parties can file claims with the vessel owners’ insurance agents.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The agencies are developing rental deferral measures to help affected businesses with their cash flow, on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Sentosa Development Corporation will also look to promote a return of footfall through marketing and social media support.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Nevertheless, SFA has been monitoring the quality of imported seafood and implementing preventive measures to ensure food safety.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our agencies will continue to press on with cleaning operations and monitor the quality of our air, food and water, as well as the impact on affected stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am also thankful for the support from service partners, volunteers and the public.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We look forward to the next and final phase of operations, where we would be inviting volunteers to help with the clean-up, so that we can nurse our cherished environment back to health as soon as possible.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I will now elaborate on the efforts taken by agencies and the community to contain and mitigate the immediate impacts of the oil spill on our coastal and marine wildlife, the impact thus far and the potential longer-term impact on biodiversity and habitats, as well as our action plans in the months to come.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: From the onset of the incident, agencies worked together and moved quickly to contain and mitigate the immediate effects and impact of the oil spill on our coastal and marine biodiversity and habitats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Affected beaches and shorelines were closed off to safeguard public health and safety, and frontline workers were deployed to clean up affected areas, such as the East Coast Park, Labrador Nature Reserve, Sentosa, as well as St John's, Lazarus and Kusu Islands.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These booms contained the spread of the oil and facilitated clean-up operations along affected beaches and shorelines.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As some oil was detected off Changi on 17 June, agencies also preemptively deployed booms around biodiversity-sensitive areas, such as at Chek Jawa Wetlands at Pulau Ubin, Coney Island and Pasir Ris Park as preventive measures.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: To ascertain the immediate impact on our marine biodiversity, agency representatives, scientists, as well as volunteers from the Friends of Marine Park and S.E.A.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Aquarium had conducted preliminary surveys at St John's Island, Sentosa, Labrador Nature Reserve, Sisters' Island Marine Park, as well as the site of the second Marine Park at the Southern part of Lazarus Island and the reef off Kusu Island, between 16 and 25 June.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Based on the visual surveys thus far, oil was sighted along the upper intertidal zones of biodiversity-sensitive sites at Labrador rocky shore, Tanjong Rimau and Serapong at Sentosa, Bendera Bay at St John's Island, Eagle Bay at Lazarus Island, as well as the outer mangrove fringes at the mouth of Berlayer Creek near Labrador Nature Reserve.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: However, the intertidal zones at other biodiversity-sensitive areas, such as Sisters' Islands Marine Park, the other Southern islands, Changi Beach Park, Pasir Ris Park and Chek Jawa Wetlands at Pulau Ubin appear to be largely unaffected.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Similarly, the mangroves at West Coast Park and Pasir Ris Park also appear to be largely unaffected.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Notwithstanding this, we will continue to monitor these sites closely.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Despite prompt veterinary care, two kingfishers unfortunately died, but the other two appear to have stabilised and we are monitoring their condition closely.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: While no significant impact on our marine biodiversity and wildlife has been observed thus far, the situation remains dynamic and there could be a time-lag between the oil spill and its effects on our biodiversity and habitats.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some of the impact on our marine and coastal ecosystems may only show up weeks or even months later, such as during spawning periods.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Assessments of the environmental impact of the oil spill on our offshore islands are therefore, also still ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Based on our experience with the oil spill that affected the intertidal and seagrass habitats at Tanah Merah back in 2010, as well as the oil spill that affected Chek Jawa Wetlands at Pulau Ubin and Changi Beach Park in 2017, while our ecosystems are resilient, they will take time to recover from such external stressors.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At Tanah Merah, the intertidal and seagrass habitats started to recover after a year and they no longer show any signs of impact from the 2010 oil spill today.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At Changi Beach Park, long-term biodiversity surveys have shown no discernible changes to the intertidal fauna before and after the oil spill in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We will closely monitor the impact of and recovery of our marine habitats and biodiversity including seagrasses, corals and aquatic wildlife, through intertidal and subtidal biodiversity surveys.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: NParks will also undertake rescue and rehabilitative efforts for affected wildlife where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Over the past few weeks, we are heartened by the public's response and support.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: An additional 2,000 have registered their interest to be kept updated on ongoing efforts and future volunteering opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Organisations, such as the Singapore Veterinary Association, World Wildlife Fund for Nature (Singapore), Singapore Canoe Federation and many more, have stepped forward to offer help in their own ways.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These volunteers have been involved in a wide range of efforts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Some joined NParks to patrol East Coast Park and West Coast Park, advising members of the public to stay away from affected beaches and areas, as well as reporting sightings of oil stains and oil-slicked wildlife for rescue and rehabilitation, if needed.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Members of the public can contact NParks' 24-hour Animal Response Centre hotline, if they encounter an oil-slicked animal.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As I shared briefly earlier, marine experts and volunteers from the Friends of Marine Park have also been carrying out surveys with NParks on St John's Island and Lazarus Island, to track the impact on biodiversity on these islands.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We are very grateful to our volunteers for their strong support, and to members of the public, nature groups and other organisations for coming together alongside our frontline workers and colleagues to mitigate the impacts of the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As we move into our next phase of managing the impact of the oil spill, we will work closely with our partners from the nature and community groups, organisations and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), and tap on their knowledge and expertise to implement an action plan to manage the impacts more effectively.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: During a recent consultation with these partners, some suggestions were raised, which will be incorporated into actionable plans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: First, we will work with various stakeholder networks to disseminate information to keep the public updated on the progress of recovery efforts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Through our partners, we hope to share information on the recovery and response operations, that can be translated into advisories and information guides for members of the public.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For instance, Otter Watch and the Bird Society of Singapore will work with us to share tips with members of the public, on the dos and don'ts when spotting oil-slicked wildlife.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Second, we will involve the wider community for coastal clean-ups and citizen patrols.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In fact, community beach clean-up groups, such as Stridy and the International Coastal Cleanup Singapore (ICCS), have already started to coordinate their respective networks, so that they can organise beach clean-ups, once we can do so.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Third, we will work with partners to tap on their expertise and skills to support wildlife rescue and recovery efforts.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Partners from Mandai Wildlife Group, Singapore Veterinary Association, ACRES and S.E.A.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Aquarium, with their own pool of veterinarians, have offered to support wildlife rescue and rehabilitation efforts, where needed.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: These efforts will inform subsequent ecological recovery action plans.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Once again, we would like to extend our gratitude to our many partners and community volunteers who have leaned forward and worked hand in hand with our colleagues in our agencies to manage the oil spill.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: With your help, we will be able to ensure that our ecosystems remain resilient.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The incident is not over yet, but we have made some good progress and we will continue to work with the community and our partners to safeguard our natural marine habitats.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There are 23 Members who have filed PQs on this topic.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You will be given priority if you have clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But before I call on hon Members for clarifications, I wish to point out Standing Order 23.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members may seek clarifications on the Ministerial Statements on this Pasir Panjang Terminal Oil Spill Incident on 14 June 2024, but no debate shall be allowed thereon.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members can seek clarifications by way of asking questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, again, because there is a lot of interest in it, I would seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise so that we can cover as many questions as possible and, at the same time, to ask the Ministers to also keep your answers short so that you can also answer as many clarifications as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Speaker, given the extremely heavy traffic in our surrounding waters and the significant environmental consequences of oil spillage accidents, I am wondering if it makes economic sense to have in-house oil spillage containment capacity rather than to contract this out to outfits such as T&T Salvage Asia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, my understanding is that the best practice response time is closer to something like two to four hours rather than the six or so hours that we engaged in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, I wonder if MOT or MSE has estimates of the total economic costs for small-, medium- and large-scale oil spills and what category does this particular incident falls under.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MPA does have quite a bit of in-house capabilities, too.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The patrol vessel, the first to arrive on the scene, was an MPA patrol vessel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MPA also has its own vessels that it has deployed.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But given the nature of oil spills and that it could happen not just in Singapore waters but also in the waters in our region, we do want to do two things.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The first is to have good collaborations with our neighbours so that in case there is an incident, there is a coordinated response, there is collaboration.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We deal with it in a coordinated manner because the oil could flow from our waters to their shores or from their waters to our shores.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is part one of how we deal with the oil spills.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Part two is that we also want to work with the industry because some of these contractors are specialised experts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some of them specialise in laying booms, some of them specialise in skimming the oil, and some of them specialise in other areas.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is important for us to not see this as a binary kind of situation, that everything has to be in-house or everything has to be outsourced.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do need to have some in-house capabilities and we do have them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is considered, I would say, on the scale, it is not the largest oil spill, but it is considered quite a serious oil spill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: All three Ministers have spoken about this point in our Ministerial Statements, about the learning points from this incident and how we can then incorporate the learning points into our SOPs, our processes, just as we have done with previous incidents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Every two years, we will do an oil spill exercise, together with the industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is alternate years – every two years, we will also do one for chemicals.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These exercises help us to be ready in case there is a chemical spill or there is an oil spill.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Minister share what is the current assessable cost of the clean-up operations?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are quite intense, a lot of manpower.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: MPA reported on 16 June, at least, that Oil Spill Response Limited (OSRL), the largest international industry-funded cooperative providing oil spill response services, was supporting the clean-up efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given OSRL's resources and expertise at hand, may I ask the Minister for Transport why was OSRL not mobilised concurrently with T&T Salvage Asia immediately after the collision to deploy the containment booms around the Marine Honour, especially with a view to reducing the deployment time and to reduce the subsequent spread of the oil spill?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My second question, bearing in mind the time required for T&T Salvage Asia to mobilise for the deployment of booms and, in particular, around the Marine Honour, would MPA consider reviewing the storage, loading and mobilisation processes of all equipment, including required containment booms, to ensure that mobilisation time can be reduced?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, will the Government consider requiring shipping terminals at locations like Pasir Panjang, Pulau Bukom, Pulau Sebarok and Jurong Island to have containment booms within easy reach of rescue vessels for quick deployment?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: My third question, has MPA contracted with T&T Salvage Asia for salvage services or for ad hoc oil spill response and recovery work?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If so, would MPA consider engaging a term contractor providing oil spill response and recovery work to deal with oil spill response and recovery work instead, to facilitate better and quicker response and mobilisation?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: T&T Salvage Asia was not the only contractor engaged by MPA.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MPA has, as I mentioned earlier, in response to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, in-house capabilities as well as a group of contractors that they work with in the industry and these are experts with many years of experience dealing with oil spills.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For T&T Salvage Asia, Captain Anuj, who is the boss of the company, was informed by his staff who were notified by MPA on the afternoon of 14 June.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think he explained this in a media interview that upon being informed about this oil spill, he then had to mobilise to load up the heavy equipment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I am sure he understands these are not lightweight, simple equipment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are heavy equipment that will require time to load up onto the vessel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is what T&T Salvage Asia did in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that process to load up the equipment took some time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Then, they had to sail from Marina South Wharves because that is the wharf that is designed to load vessels like the T&T Salvage Asia vessel to be able to deal with incidents like oil spills.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is a reason why we chose Marina South Wharves, because if you think about the entire anchorage in the southern part of Singapore, you have from Tuas to Pasir Panjang and all the way to the eastern anchorages.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Captain Anuj explained during his media interview, it was at night.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, he and his crew did their best to deploy the heavy containment boom as quickly as they can.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But it took them till the next morning before they could fully deploy them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There will be tidal currents, there will be waves and these will carry the oil and it will float elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the purpose of deploying T&T Salvage Asia is not to try and "fence in" the oil.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is to try and have a preventive measure around the damaged vessel because, let us not forget, there is still a lot of oil inside the damaged vessel that has not been released and spilled into the sea.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we wanted to make sure that in case there is further spillage, there is a preventive measure around the damaged vessel to deal with that scenario.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The next thing that has to be done is MPA and the contractors, together with our agencies, would have to try and locate where the oil patches, the spilled oil, are floating to, because you need to be able to locate it, then you can deal with it through the skimmers and the laying of booms to try and deal with the oil at sea.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Please do allow me to ask two supplementary questions or clarifications to the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, I would like to thank the Ministers and the various Ministries for coming out very fast in terms of communications and also the various groups that have helped to quickly come out with the ongoing works to clean up the beaches and the waters around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think Minister mentioned just now a very important thing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In regard to the oil spill, it may not be localised and it could be coming from outside the region.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am aware that there is an ASEAN cooperation mechanism for joint oil spills.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am wondering whether Minister can share a bit about that, including how the Revolving Fund Committee works, in terms of allocation of responsibilities if it happens abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we know, Singapore is a maritime hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Any oil spills slightly out of Singapore's waters could actually come in and affects Sisters Island and even Chek Jawa and other parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, it is in regard to my original PQ which is about the penalties under the Act.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Essentially, whether sufficient deterrent will be there, especially with us as a maritime hub?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If the findings of the investigation later turn out that it is not the fault of the bunker vessel, then the bunker vessel owners can have the right to then submit their own claims against the other party, which caused the allision.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is the second part of Mr Saktiandi's question.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The first part, indeed, as I mentioned earlier in my response to Assoc Prof James Lim, we recognise that this is not something that Singapore can deal with or our neighbours can deal with alone, because the oil can float from one part of the sea to another part of the sea across the boundaries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why we have, when we were notified of this oil spill, alerted our Malaysian and Indonesian counterparts, and we also provided updates to them along the way and offered our assistance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think this is a process that has worked well over the years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This mechanism that we have, together with the cooperation that we have built up with the industry, remains a very important part of our overall preparedness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because as I mentioned in my Statement earlier, it is not possible to completely eliminate the risk of oil spills and therefore we have to be ready that if it occurs, and it will occur from time to time, we are able to respond effectively.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is can the Minister for Transport share further details on the response time requirements for the different levels of oil spill severity, on the different types of resource owners, whether it is the boom operator or otherwise?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, just like how for us National Servicemen, there are different kind of requirements in terms of the manning, depending on the operational demands of the different units.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, have the current operators performed to required response time and effectiveness standards in the twice-yearly oil spill response exercise?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are they stress-tested, and will the Minister consider tightening the standards and conducting such exercises annually in light of this incident?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The learning points from this incident, certainly I think as I mentioned earlier, we will take on board and see how we can further enhance our processes, our SOPs, and we will also factor this in in the regular exercises that we conduct.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The next exercise for the oil spill will be in October this year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As for standards, it is difficult to have a precise single number.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And I hope Mr Chua can appreciate why, because every oil spill is different, depending on the scale, depending on the nature, depending on the geography, the time to respond to the oil spill can vary from oil spill to oil spill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In some instances, the oil may not float very far away.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In some instances, it may float further away.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In some instances, like I mentioned, the oil density makes it easier to detect because it floats on the surface.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In this case, it was an added challenge because this oil has similar density as the seawater, so it could go below the surface.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And then subsequently, the deployment of the vessels to keep track of the oil and then to start cleaning it up.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have received positive responses from industry experts from different parts of the world who commented that Singapore's response in this particular incident, and I am sure they are comparing based on their years of experience with other incidents around the world, our response, in their words, was "extremely fast".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan, you raised your hand earlier?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I thank the Ministers for their comprehensive statements about our timely, competent and coordinated response so far.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But just to build on Minister Chee's point about not all oil spills being the same, and at the same time, this oil spill was significant.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is not the largest in our history.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And to my question that I filed earlier about our contingency plans, I would like to ask the Minister if our contingency plans are sized for a much larger oil spill that is a lot closer to our shoreline, making a full frontal impact on our shoreline?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Do we have the assets and the methods that are needed to deal with an oil spill of such a scale and with a full frontal impact on our shoreline?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And of course, as I mentioned earlier, the partnership with our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think if there is a very major oil spill, whether it is very near to our shores or further away, closer to our neighbours or in international waters, I think this is the response that will be most effective.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Not relying only on one single party, but tapping on the resources and the assets of all the different partners within the ecosystem and rehearsing this regularly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Keeping the links warm, keeping the SOPs well run so that everyone knows their roles and their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have some supplementary questions for the Minister for Transport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note the Minister's earlier reply that booms cannot contain 100% of the oil and he feels the contractors performed to par.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But how much oil had already dispersed beyond the collision site by the time the booms were deployed 15 hours after the collision?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And could the oil slick have been better contained if the booms were deployed earlier?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does Singapore have any such regulations and if not, are there any plans to enact them?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, I do not think the Minister has fully answered my Question No 14 for Oral Answer and Question No 67 for Written Answer, which he said he would cover in the Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But since Mr Giam raised it again, let me try to make another attempt to explain.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is therefore not the correct response to try and use the containment booms to "fence in" the oil.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because as I explained earlier, there is still a lot of oil left that we are now in the process of safely removing from the damaged vessel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think this is an important point to clarify, so that we are on the same page.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And as I explained earlier, then what do you do with the oil that has been spilled and is floating away?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The operations are then mounted to try and track and confirm the location of these large oil patches, so that you can then send out other types of vessels, the skimmers, to try and remove this oil, collect this oil.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And then also to lay booms in certain areas to try and soak up this oil.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But you first need to know where these oil patches are, where it is floating to and MPA deployed a multi-pronged approach using a variety of information sources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, that is how the oil spill response is done, not just in Singapore, but internationally.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The US requirement that Mr Giam mentioned is not something which is done in major ports.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There was an earlier media article which quoted someone – they did not give the name, they called this person Captain A from the industry, who asked if we could put booms around the vessels in our anchorages.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The article also mentioned that this was done in the Netherlands.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But when we checked with the Port of Rotterdam, which is also a major port, they said no, they do not have this practice of requiring booms to be placed around vessels.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because we have so many ships in our anchorages and they are not just static, they are also coming in and going out, it is just not practical and feasible to take that approach.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I hope that answers the two questions that Mr Gerald Giam raised.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Gerald Giam also said that he has some further questions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I was just flipping through earlier and I saw that one of them – just to seek Mr Gerald Giam's confirmation, is the Member asking about the height of the booms, freeboard and skirt?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Is that one of the questions that you want me to answer?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: That is one of the questions, as well as Question No 67 for Written Answer.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On Mr Giam's question for written answer, for storage tanks, we have sufficient storage tank capacity for the operations, because the storage tanks, when you put it on the vessel, when you go out to sea and you skim the oil, collect the oil, you do have enough capacity, but if the volume in the tanks were to increase, you can come back to shore and use a new tank, replace with a new tank and then you go out again.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This was not a constraint in this particular response.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It was not due to lack of storage tank capacity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What was challenging, and I explained this in my Ministerial Statement, was it took some time to locate where the oil patches, this is the estimated 400 tonnes that floated away.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It took us some time to be able to confirm the location of these large oil patches that floated away due to a variety of reasons that I have explained earlier – bad weather in the initial period and after that nightfall, and in this particular case, because the density of the oil was quite similar to seawater, it could go below the water surface, which then makes detection more difficult.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And when that is identified and confirmed, MPA then sent out the skimmers to collect this oil.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our cleaners, very often, work under trying conditions and it is heartening to know that safety measures and SOPs have been put in place to ensure their safety and well-being.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Arguably, the cleaning up of oil spills would mean even more challenging conditions such as blistering heat, humid weather and the constant fight against time to contain and to remove the spill.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Does MSE have measures put in place to ensure that all our cleaning workers are provided with ample rest and whether certain groups of workers are excluded from the strenuous clean-up deployments, such as workers with pre-existing health conditions?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We would like to remind all our service providers to adhere to the recommendations from the various agencies that are looking at workplace safety and to pay extra attention to the well-being of the workers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Personally, I met some of them when I was visiting the affected beaches.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I never fail to ask them, "Are you given rest?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Are you given time out to have your hydration?" And the answer has been, "Yes".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I think that is something that is of priority and I would like to assure Members that we are always work with our contractors to make sure that their workers' well-being is also looked after.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In response to part of my PQ on what recourse workers have should they have or are suspected to be suffering from ill effects due to exposure, while I acknowledge the Minister's earlier points about no anomalies being detected during air quality monitoring, can the Minister clarify whether there were any reports received about health concerns from our workers and now our volunteers given that they have started to be deployed and what recourse do they have should they suffer from or are suspected to be suffering from ill effects due to both dermal and inhalation exposure?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have a couple of clarifications for the Minister for National Development.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, I do not think I heard the answer to part of my question about whether the oil spill has affected plans for a second marine park in the Southern Islands.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How much is the total cost expected to be for these studies and research projects?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: On workers who are involved in cleaning, I will clarify that there are mainly two categories of workers who are involved.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One is general cleaners and they are involved in very basic but back-breaking work at the foreshore of the beaches, basically to clean up the oil leaks as well as the contaminated sand.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The ratio, I would imagine that they would conform to the foreign workers ratio of general cleaners.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They would be supervised as usual and, as I mentioned in my speech earlier on, contractors, their employers have been advised to adhere to giving them the adequate and appropriate protective equipment.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There is also another type who are involved in specialised cleaning.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Those will come from contractors who are engaged to handle such cleaning of the hard-to-reach places and they would have gone through their own internal training programme.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some of them are actually our local workers with experience in the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) and Singapore Police Force (SPF).

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They have now joined this contractor, basically handling emergency responses, such as oil spill and other incidents and crises.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They are very, very competent, very experienced, putting their experience from SCDF and SPF to good use and they are obviously very mindful and aware, high degree of awareness of the environment that they are working in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And secondly, in terms of the total cost of monitoring and research, we are still working out the research questions and methodology, processes and locations of these works.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The exact figure will be worked out in due course.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond the workers and specialised professionals who have been really hard at work, I think we have also been able to engage some of the researchers who have specialised skills.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, Minister Desmond Lee mentioned Friends of Marine Park, who went out, I think, maybe the day or two, really soon after, to engage in the work and there are many more volunteers, as the Ministers have pointed out, who are really interested to come forward, whether those who kayak out at sea or those who do beach clean-ups.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think they are looking forward to maybe when the next phase might be so, that they can really galvanise and come together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there a rough indication how long more this will take?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And will there be any sort of maybe training or briefing at a very high level to be able to equip them with the information on how they can best help with the clean-up?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second is, beyond the wanting to help.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think many also want accountability in due course to be able to hear more as to how the collision happened and whether the parties responsible or the parties involved will be taking accountability.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We would very much like to involve all Singaporeans who are willing to help us rehabilitate our beautiful beaches.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Please be assured that when we do so, when we mobilise the volunteers, we will think through, we will put through procedures that involve training as well as briefing, as well as resourcing with adequate protective equipment, so that we can all do so safely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By 16 June, some of the Friends of Marine Park had already been galvanised to do a survey of some of the Southern Islands.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They helped us monitor impact and to identify shorelines and habitats that have been affected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some have been mobilised for more specialised works pertaining to the environment, habitats, biodiversity and wildlife.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And on 21 June, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng and I met many members of the community, green groups, environmental groups, IHLs, researchers, organisations, who wanted to support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These are all areas where we engage stakeholders, including those who are more specialised with skills that they can offer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we work very closely with them to ensure that in carrying out these operations, this is all done safely and securely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In response to the Member's second question on accountability, as Minister Chee Hong Tat had mentioned earlier in his answer, investigations are ongoing, even as operations to clean-up are in their second phase.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is some more work to be done, so allow the investigation to run its course before we address the broader issue of accountability in different aspects.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, I would like to ask how effective was the predictive modelling used by MPA when trying to predict where the oil spill would move, based on tidal predictions and real-time weather data, which would then have informed and guided their decisions on where to deploy the skimmers and the oil booms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My second question is regarding one of my PQs, which asked whether the whole-of-Government response is coordinated with those of the non-governmental organisations (NGOs), including the volunteer groups.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I think the Minister mentioned that there are regular oil spill exercises and the next one being in October this year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My question is, are these NGOs invited to participate in the exercises, including the volunteer groups; and if not, would they be invited to do so?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But, as I mentioned earlier, we do not rely only on one source, because this is a highly fluid situation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is not something that, I think, any single source of information will give you the full picture.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What MPA has done is to use a multi-pronged approach from drones, satellite imagery, modelling is one of the sources of info and the old-fashioned way, which is visual sighting by personnel at sea and also by our personnel who are on land, looking out for signs of the oil.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think that is one area where it is a continuous improvement process.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will be happy to work with researchers, with scientists, to see how we can take on board the learning points and further finetune our modelling.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The whole-of-Government approach and involving our industry partners that we do regularly, every two years, oil spill exercise; every two years, chemical spill exercise.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That one, so far, has been more Government agencies plus industry players.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The reason is because, it is dealing with the response out at sea; and also dealing with the use of different sources of information, running through different processes, looking at the different assets, the different kinds of vessels that you can use.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Do we want to involve the volunteers who would not likely go out to sea but more likely will be helping on land?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think that is something which we will be happy to take a look at together with the Ministry of National Development and MSE colleagues.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think I have covered all those Members who have filed PQs on this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will now move to the other Members.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many businesses that have been affected adversely by this oil spill incident.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am glad to hear from the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment that rental assistance is currently being discussed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Apart from rental costs, businesses face other costs as well, for example, wages for their employees.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the Government looking into possibly helping the small businesses further, for example, in seeking compensation and providing some financial schemes, like, bridging loans on preferential terms, to tie them over until they have received their compensation?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As I mentioned earlier in my speech, the person to contact, I think you can find it as public information.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Those that have agencies, whether it is NParks or SDC, as your landlords, I am sure they have already reached out to you.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some of the businesses are completely unable to operate because they were operating sea-based activities, while others that are operating on the back shore of the beaches, they have been able to resume.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some of them have very much resumed to pre-spill days, some of them have not.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I think we cannot take a standard approach or one-standard-solution for the businesses.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Government agencies will be very prepared to listen to the plight of the businesses and see how we can best help them.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I just want to follow on the question from the business side of things.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Minister Chee mentioned that there will always be lessons learned from each incident and I am sure post the incident, there will be further step-up measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask whether as the Transport Minister or the Minister-in-charge of Trade Relations, whether post the oil spill incident, would we see increase in the cost for shipping and in the maritime sectors in Singapore and hence any wider implications to the economy?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second question is for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, whether the oil spill incident will have a bearing on our push to decarbonise the maritime sector?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Whether, as the industry moves toward hydrogen and ammonia-powered ships, are we gearing up our capabilities to prevent as well as potentially deal with, the effects of allisions or collisions of such ships?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The first question, the point that is important for us to bear in mind is: yes, there are some learning points that we can certainly look at incorporating into our processes and SOPs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is something that we do after every incident, so that we benefit from the process of deriving the learning points that will enable us to deal with future incidents with greater confidence.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Having said that, I think it is important for us to bear in mind that the overall response by our agencies, industry partners and volunteers to this oil spill on 14 June was a prompt and effective one.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is something which, precisely because our response to the oil spill was swift and effective, I think it did not damage our reputation as an international hub port and maritime centre.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Unlike, for example, what is happening at the Red Sea, where that kind of incident, yes, that will affect global shipping costs, because ships have to then detour and go a longer distance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, in response to Mr Liang's question, I think we cannot 100% eliminate the risk of oil spills happening.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But how we respond to the oil spills, I think that is how can differentiate Singapore from other ports around the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Liang's second question is about the future, because we do have a plan to decarbonise our maritime sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if you talk about the larger ocean-going vessels – container ships, tankers – those, they cannot run on batteries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I state in that order, because that is the level of readiness at this point in time for the global shipping industry.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With LNG, of course, it is the most well-established amongst all these different alternatives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Methanol, they have done some tests, but it is not quite ready for large-scale commercial deployment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have done some tests as well with some of the industry players.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ammonia as well, we have done some initial pilots and tests.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Why we are doing all these tests and pilots, is because we need to confirm and understand the risks involved.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Then, we can develop our safety protocols that, in the future, you have more ships now using ammonia or more ships now using methanol.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: How do we deal with those kinds of different types of fuel?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because the risks are quite different from a traditional oil spill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you have an ammonia leak, it will not be going into the water like an oil spill and then floating away, carried by tidal currents and waves.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It may potentially go into the air and you have a plume cloud.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is a very different kind of risk compared to how we deal with the conventional oil spills.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, Mr Speaker, a more elaborate answer, but I think it is an important point to clarify because we remain committed to looking at how we can bring on board these newer fuels, because decarbonising the maritime industry remains our goal.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we want to find a way to do it safely, so that we are able to make progress.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can I confirm that the Minister said just now, in response to my supplementary question, that the purpose of the containment boom around the damaged vessel is not meant to try to catch the oil that has already been spilt into the sea and that it is not the correct response to try and use the containment booms to fence in the oil around the damaged vessel?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: If so, what is the purpose of deploying containment booms?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The Minister said that, how we respond to oil spills can make a difference to our reputation around the world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does the Minister not agree that the earlier the booms are deployed, the better?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Because even if the booms cannot completely fence in the oil, they can prevent a large amount of the oil from spreading faster and this would reduce the amount and cost of the clean-up needed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, are we looking to increasing our capacity for faster boom deployment in future oil spills?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What I am sharing with Mr Giam is the international practice and the industry's response to oil spills.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, these are methods and processes that have been developed over the years by experts and this is how it is done internationally, not just in Singapore but also in other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, this is not an opinion that we are debating over.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What I am sharing is the international practice.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But allow me to come back to the concern that Mr Giam raised, which is, the sooner you deploy, the better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is no disagreement that faster is better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, knowing that boom deployment requires time, even if you are able to do it very quickly – because the weather was good, it was daytime, you were able to do it more quickly – it is still going to have a time lag.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: From the point of the allision and the oil spilling in a large amount into the sea, by the time the booms are fully deployed, even under the best circumstances, there will be a gap.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is to deal with what is remaining in the vessel, to prevent further spillage, in case it comes out, because there is no guarantee that the oil will stay inside the damaged vessel.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It could spill again and, if in that scenario, when your boom is up, then, yes, you will be able to contain that amount of oil, the subsequent spillage, better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there is no disagreement with Mr Giam, that speed is important and faster is better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I also hope that Mr Giam understands that, even under the best circumstances, some tasks are just not possible, not practical.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In this case, it is not possible to try and "fence in" the oil around the damaged vessel because it has already been spilled and it will be carried by the currents and the waves away from the location side.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Alright, we have spent almost an hour on clarifications and I do not see any more hands being raised.
